learningObjectives.text: Identify the central source-grounded idea in Odysseus: Cunning and Return.
Connect the idea to the cited source, genre, and version.

odyssey.author: Homer
odyssey.excerpt: COUNCIL—MINERVA’S VISIT TO ITHACA—THE CHALLENGE FROM TELEMACHUS TO THE SUITORS. Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover
odyssey.note: Verbatim local text with whitespace normalized. Lesson analysis is interpretation, not part of this quotation.

narrativeBlocks.title: A different heroic engine
narrativeBlocks.body: The Odyssey opens by calling its hero ingenious. Its story is built from wandering, disguise, intelligence, patience, and return.

narrativeBlocks.title: Cunning is more than deception
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotations are available under the source buttons. They are translations, not the lesson author’s wording. Compare the work and locator before drawing conclusions.

narrativeBlocks.title: Return as achievement
narrativeBlocks.body: His heroism is measured by getting home and recovering identity—a different arc from Achilles’ public honor.

narrativeBlocks.title: Ingenuity is tested under pressure
narrativeBlocks.body: Odysseus’ cleverness is not decoration. The Odyssey repeatedly asks whether intelligence can survive temptation, disguise, exhaustion, and delayed recognition.

narrativeBlocks.title: Keep the heroic models separate
narrativeBlocks.body: Achilles’ story asks what honor costs when rage is unleashed. Odysseus’ story asks what endurance and self-control can recover. Comparing them is useful only if their different engines remain visible.

quiz.prompt: What makes cunning an incomplete guarantee of success?

choices.text: Judgement and restraint still matter alongside clever plans.
It removes the need to regain a household.
